questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Wageningen University & Research has a great reputation in sustainability and life sciences, which fits my studies really well. I also liked the very international student community and the fact that the Netherlands is a safe, well-organized country with easy travel around Europe. Overall, Wageningen felt like a welcoming, student-friendly place to live and study.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I would say it was fairly easy, there was a lot of emails with information. But you get the information really last minute.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: When I arrived, I received mostly general information and practical advice from Wageningen University & Research, like guidance on housing, registration, transport, and daily life in the Netherlands. It wasn’t very detailed, but it was helpful for settling in and understanding how things work here.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It was a bit difficult because there is a housing crisis in the Netherlands, but still doable. I found my place through Facebook housing groups, which are very active. Some other exchange students found housing via Idealis. My recommendation is to start early, check online daily, and apply to many places.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Living off campus is common, but you need to be proactive. Join multiple Facebook groups, be quick to reply, and don’t be too picky at first. Also, be aware of scams and never send money without a contract or viewing. Even though it’s competitive, if you search actively, it should be possible to find something.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *

How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: The registration process at Wageningen University & Research was pretty easy and straightforward through the online system. The website guides you step by step, and exchange students are often recommended to follow a minor, which is kind of pre-planned and makes course selection easier. You do need to check yourself that classes don’t overlap.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: There was good support available if needed. You can email the exchange coordinators, and they are helpful with questions about courses, registration, or issues with learning agreements. The website itself also explains most things clearly.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Overall, I was successful in registering for the courses I wanted. Not all courses are open to exchange students, but there are still many options, and almost all courses are taught in English.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: My advice would be to double-check course codes and schedules after registering, especially for your online learning agreement. Make sure your courses don’t overlap, and honestly pick courses you’re interested in. If you’re unsure about anything, don’t hesitate to contact the exchange coordinators for help.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I took a mix of Bachelor- and Master-level courses at WUR. Overall, the level varied quite a lot. Some first-year Bachelor courses felt much easier than what I was used to, mainly because students start specializing earlier here. At the same time, higher-level courses were more demanding and required continuous work. The workload was generally high, even when the academic level felt lower, because of many assignments and group projects.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Compared to UCPH, teaching at Wageningen is much more focused on case studies, group work, and practical projects rather than lectures and final exams. There are fewer traditional exams and more continuous assessment, which means more weekly work but less exam pressure. It felt more applied and hands-on than at UCPH.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend choosing a minor (course package) within a subject you’re genuinely interested in, as it gives structure and coherence to your semester. In general, courses with case studies and group projects are very engaging and help you apply theory to real-world problems. I’d also recommend avoiding very basic first-year courses unless you need them, as they may feel too easy compared to higher-level options.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: One unexpected cost was how expensive public transport in the Netherlands is. I ended up spending more than expected on buses and trains, especially at the beginning before settling in. I suggest buying a used bike, saves you a lot of money.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Overall, daily expenses were higher than I expected, especially groceries and transport. Public transport in particular was surprisingly expensive, so I would strongly recommend getting a bike as soon as possible, it’s much cheaper and also the most common way students get around. Groceries are kinda the same price as in denmark.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: At WUR there are a lot of cultural, sports, and social activities, honestly almost anything you can think of. There are many student sports clubs, cultural associations, parties, and events, and most of them are also open to exchange students, which makes it easy to get involved.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I’d really recommend joining ESN Wageningen. It’s a great space for exchange students to meet each other, and they organize lots of events, parties, and social activities. They also sometimes arrange trips to other cities or even other countries, which is a fun and easy way to travel while meeting people.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: I’d recommend traveling around the Netherlands and nearby countries—cities like Amsterdam, Utrecht, or Rotterdam are easy to reach. Because the Netherlands is so well connected, it’s also perfect for weekend trips to places like Belgium or Germany. Even staying local is nice too, biking around Wageningen and enjoying nature is very underrated.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was pretty easy overall to adjust at WUR. The environment is very international, so you don’t really feel out of place as an exchange student. Day-to-day life felt comfortable quite quickly.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Honestly, I ended up making mostly international and exchange student friends, mainly because everyone is actively looking to meet new people. Dutch students can be friendly but tend to already have their social circles and keep a bit to themselves. Joining student associations, group projects, or social events helps, but it’s totally normal if most of your friends end up being international.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: One thing I noticed was that Dutch students start university earlier than in Denmark, so many of them are quite young, which is sometimes noticeable in group work or social settings. I also never really learned Dutch, since almost everything was in English and I mostly spoke English with other internationals.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I really appreciated how open, direct, and international the environment is. Almost everyone speaks English, which makes life very easy as an exchange student. I also liked the relaxed student lifestyle and the strong biking culture—it makes everyday life simple and enjoyable.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Remember you’re not only there to study—make time to explore the Netherlands and travel around Europe.
Don’t stress too much about making friends; it happens naturally, especially with other exchange and international students.
Be prepared to be independent, there is help available, but you’ll also have to figure out many things on your own.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Even though WUR is very organized, daily life still requires initiative. Join activities, talk to people, and use the connections you make, other students are often your best source of help and advice.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting people from all over the world and building friendships through shared experiences. Living in such an international environment really broadens your perspective, both academically and personally.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Probably finding the right balance between studying and enjoying the exchange. I sometimes focused a bit too much on academics and had to remind myself to slow down and enjoy the experience outside university as well.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
